This video presents a serious “systemic capture” argument: that the relationship between government institutions, regulators, senior bureaucrats, the judiciary and large corporate groups deserves much closer public scrutiny.

But there is an important distinction between facts, allegations and conclusions.

The video points to a series of former senior officials who, after leaving public office, subsequently joined corporate boards or advisory positions. That pattern of post-retirement appointments can be independently examined through corporate filings, government records and official biographies. The appointment itself is a fact; claiming that it proves institutional capture is an allegation or interpretation that requires further evidence. 

The uncomfortable question is not:

“Why did these individuals join private companies?”

Public officials are legally entitled to pursue careers after retirement, subject to applicable rules.

The deeper question is:

Did their previous regulatory, administrative or judicial responsibilities create conflicts of interest when they subsequently entered corporate positions?

And if potential conflicts existed:

Were cooling-off rules applicable?

Were disclosures made?

Were recusals required?

Were appointments independently reviewed?

Did any former official later advise an entity over which they previously exercised regulatory authority?

Were post-retirement restrictions followed?

These are verifiable questions, not conspiracy theories.

The video alleges that regulatory settlements and legal mechanisms can sometimes reduce the public visibility of corporate wrongdoing. That claim should not automatically be treated as established fact.

For example, SEBI has recently closed proceedings against several Adani Group companies following settlements concerning alleged disclosure and audit-related violations. The companies settled the proceedings without admitting or denying the allegations. That distinction matters. 

Likewise, the video raises questions about the KG-D6 gas controversy and other corporate-regulatory disputes. Those matters have their own complex legal and factual histories and should be judged from court records, regulatory orders and official documents—not simply from a political narrative.

The most important issue is therefore not whether every allegation in this video is correct.

It is whether India possesses sufficiently strong institutional safeguards to detect and prevent conflicts of interest before public trust is damaged.

A democracy needs:

Independent regulators.
Transparent decision-making.
Strong conflict-of-interest rules.
Effective cooling-off periods.
Public disclosure of relevant relationships.
Independent scrutiny of regulatory settlements.
And accountability that applies equally to powerful corporations and ordinary citizens.

Because suspicion is not proof.

But unanswered, credible questions can become a serious institutional problem.

And that is precisely why every allegation should be tested against documentary evidence rather than dismissed—or accepted—on political loyalty.

Don't ask citizens to choose between conspiracy theories and blind faith.

Give them the documents.

Show them the orders.

Publish the regulatory reasoning.

Disclose the relationships.

Let independent institutions investigate.

In a democracy, transparency is not an inconvenience to power. It is the mechanism by which power earns legitimacy.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order.

2. *STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Those Protesting Against NEET Paper Leak Make A Website Which Then Gets Compromised, Personal Details Of Volunteers Leaked : 
The Joke That Is CJP

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

One of the simplest ways for a government or large authority to restrict access to certain websites across a region is DNS-level blocking through ISP resolvers. In India, this is exactly how most website restrictions are enforced. By default, your device relies on the ISP’s DNS resolver, so DNS-based blocking takes effect automatically. However, this can often be bypassed by switching to third-party DNS resolvers such as Cloudflare(1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8).

Compared to this, China is much stricter, as China deploys censorship at multiple network layers simultaneously, making circumvention exponentially harder.

China’s Great Firewall works by checking internet traffic at many different levels, not just DNS. It uses Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) to look inside data packets as they travel through the network. It performs SNI inspection to read the domain name you’re trying to reach during the HTTPS handshake, which is why simply switching DNS doesn’t bypass it.

It also blocks the entire IP ranges of platforms like Google, Facebook, and YouTube at the router level, so even if you obtain the correct IP through a service like Cloudflare DNS, the connection is immediately dropped.

The system carries out active probing, where it tests servers that appear to be VPNs and blocks them quickly if confirmed. Finally, it uses protocol fingerprinting to study traffic patterns such as packet timing and size to detect VPN or proxy traffic even when the data is fully encrypted.

China is highly dedicated to preventing people from using foreign websites and instead pushes them to use their own.

Your app didn’t crash because of a bug. It crashed because the Indian government decided to block your backend.

Starting February 24th, https://t.co/cpotyIe5BS became unreachable across major Indian ISPs. Supabase later confirmed this was due to a ministry order. No prior notice. No public explanation. No transition window.

Jio. Airtel. ACT Fibernet. All started DNS-poisoning Supabase domains, redirecting API calls to a sinkhole IP. Every app running on Supabase in India (auth, database, edge functions, real-time) went dark for millions of users. Reports suggest Firebase Hosting is facing similar disruptions.

Thousands of startups, student projects, hackathon builds, production SaaS apps. Blocked. No “here’s 90 days to migrate.” Nothing.

Supabase had to publicly tag Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on X just to get someone to talk to them: “Supabase is used by millions of developers worldwide, and millions of users in India are currently unable to access our platform. Could we talk to someone in your team about this?”

Silence from MeitY. Silence from the Minister. Silence from every ISP.

Supabase is not a social media platform. It’s a PostgreSQL database wrapper with auth, storage, and APIs. Its users are engineers building software. There is no obvious legal or content-based reason to block it.

And this isn’t the first time. Medium blocked on Jio/Airtel in Oct 2025. Linktree blocked without explanation. BSNL blocked Dailymotion and Telegram links in Aug 2025. ACT Fibernet blocked TheMovieDB. Ubuntu mirrors and Cloudflare R2 hit before that.

Critical internet infrastructure keeps getting caught in opaque, unaccountable blocking orders. No public reasoning. No appeals process. No distinction between a piracy site and a developer tool.

The workaround? Switch DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. Use a VPN. Proxy backend traffic through custom domains so you’re not exposed to ISP blocks.

But think about what we’re saying. We’re telling Indian developers: “Your government might randomly block your backend, so architect around that.” That’s not a healthy ecosystem. That’s building on a minefield.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

East took them. The West can want them. The volume, on his book, is not there.

Those are not the same chair.

2 · ROOTS (PRIMARY ORIGIN)
Potash is potassium salt. Agriculture uses muriate of potash (MOP / KCl). USGS tables often print K2O equivalent. Those units are not interchangeable without a named conversion. This page keeps them on separate rails.

The Prairie root
The world’s largest known potash reserve sits under Saskatchewan. Natural Resources Canada: all ten active Canadian mines are in that province. 2024 Canadian MOP production about 25 million tonnes KCl, about 32.8 percent of world mine output. Four operators: Nutrien, Mosaic, Compass Minerals, K+S Potash Canada.
Nutrien (PotashCorp + Agrium, 2018) holds the large Saskatchewan set: Rocanville, Allan, Lanigan, Cory, Patience Lake, Vanscoy. Public nameplate on that set is far above operational capability. Rocanville is the giant. Product moves on rail to Vancouver and Portland as well as south into the U.S. corn belt.
Mosaic: Esterhazy (K3 ramp) and Belle Plaine. Mosaic sold Brazil and New Mexico potash mines in 2025. Saskatchewan became even more of that firm’s potash body.
K+S: Bethune. Compass: smaller Canadian stamp.
Dead Canadian leaf: the former PCS New Brunswick mine stopped in 2016 and closed in 2018 because Saskatchewan was cheaper. The Atlantic door on the Canadian side is already a fallen leaf. The living door is the prairie.

The U.S. farm root
USGS MCS 2026: U.S. marketable production in 2025 on the order of 0.5 million tonnes K2O-class; imports for consumption about 5.6 million tonnes K2O-class; apparent consumption about 5.9. Import dependence about 92 percent of use in 2025. Canada about 79 percent of those imports across the recent window; Russia about 12 percent. Fertilizer takes about 85 percent of imported tonnes. New Mexico still mines. Montana / North Dakota hold deep Williston-basin resource that is not this year’s silo. No substitute exists in the USGS sentence.

The Minsk root
Belaruskali at Soligorsk. State cash cow. USGS 2024/2025 class: Belarus on the order of 5–6 million tonnes K2O-equivalent mine output; world share historically near a tenth to a sixth depending on the year and the unit. 2024 company/industry notes put Belarus near 7.1 million tonnes product-class and about 6.4 million tonnes exported that year. Before the wall the U.S. historically took on the order of 0.5–1.0 million tonnes a year from Minsk. That trickle is not a roof for a U.S. farm that eats Canadian millions.

The Baltic dead leaf
For nearly two decades, red grit rode Lithuanian rail into Klaipeda. Belaruskali held about 30 percent of the cargo terminal. Lithuania terminated the LTG Cargo / Belaruskali transit contract effective 1 February 2022 after U.S. sanctions packages of 9 August and 2 December 2021. Vilnius called further cooperation a national-security problem. Minsk answered by blocking Lithuanian oil-product and fertilizer transit the other way. The living west door closed. Minsk said the ore would go through St. Petersburg and Murmansk. Distance rose. Margin fell. Price later compensated some of that, not all of the geography.

The Russian pipe that grew in the dead leaf’s place
Kommersant-class soil: in 2025 Belarus shipped about 11.9 million tonnes of potassium chloride through Russian terminals — Bronka about half, Ust-Luga about a quarter, rail to China/CIS and St. Petersburg houses the rest. A Belarusian deep-water idea at Lavna / Murmansk (tens of millions of tonnes class, talk of 2028) remains a seed, not a dock. On this same Monday Reuters reports Russian Baltic and Arctic fertilizer terminals being adapted the other way — toward grain — after Black Sea disruption. The pipe that was supposed to be Minsk’s west door is itself being asked to carry other cargo. That is a cousin. It is not a U.S. farm schedule.

The sanction-and-prisoner root
2020 crackdown. 2021 U.S. packages on Belaruskali and then BPC. Land and rail given to Russia for the war on Ukraine. March 2026: OFAC removes Belaruskali, Belarusian Potash Company, Agrorozkvit after prisoner releases. Envoy John Coale. 16 September 2026: twenty-five more prisoners; further company relief on that track. The mineral came back into the American room as a chip. A chip is not a cargo.

3 · PUBLIC OBJECT THIS MONDAY (AUDITED SOIL)
Trump, Truth Social, 21 September 2026:
The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.

Lukashenko, same date, office text from the meeting with customs chair Uladzimir Arlouski:
Exports shifted east. Even if we wanted to supply Western markets, we simply do not have the volume. It is all under contract.

Eleven days earlier, 11 September, the same Lukashenko said sales to the U.S. had resumed after sanctions came off, that a vessel loading for the United States was nearing completion, and that more than $40 million is still “stuck” in the American banking system. Resumed is not spare. A frozen forty million is a bill, not a shipload. Some volumes becoming available is ο.

China customs, January–August 2026: 2.58 million tonnes of potassium chloride from Belarus. India and Indonesia sit on the same eastward book he named.

Canadian potash remains exempt from the new U.S. tariffs. The fight with Ottawa is loud. The mineral was left off the blade because the farm cannot eat a speech.

StoneX to Reuters this Monday: doubts Belarusian tonnes will move U.S. price or volume in a material way. Analyst, not a hymn.

Scott Moe, Saskatchewan, same afternoon: buying “blood potash” from Belarus supports Russian aggression. Forty-plus countries still sanction Minsk on that war. He asked whether ore shipped through Russia would be cheaper, cleaner, or more ethical than ore from next door.

Dominic LeBlanc and Nutrien: no immediate comment. Silence is not assent. It is a waiting room.
Fertilizer Canada: Canada has been a reliable supplier to North American farms for decades. Stamp, not seal.

4 · LIVING BRANCH · JANSEN
BHP Jansen, about 140 km east of Saskatoon. Stage 1 first production still aimed at mid-calendar 2027, about 4.15–4.2 million tonnes KCl a year after ramp. Stage 2 first production slipped toward late FY2031; combined target about 8.5 million tonnes. Capex has been revised upward more than once (Stage 1 now in the US$8.4 billion class including contingencies). Jansen is a future roof-thickener. It is not this Monday’s silo. Do not MERGE 2027 into 21 September.

5 · FALLEN LEAVES THAT STILL CARRY DNA
New Brunswick PCS: closed. Proves Canadian production concentrates where the geology and the cost curve live — Saskatchewan — not where a speech points.
Mosaic Carlsbad: shrunk; Mosaic’s potash body is now almost entirely the prairie.
Klaipeda terminal share: a dead western tap. DNA still visible in every extra kilometre of Russian rail.
2021–22 price spike after the wall: the last time Minsk left the Western book, Saskatchewan and Russia filled. Traders this year priced Belarus’s OFAC return without a crash. Re-entry was already in the tape. A Monday post does not replay 2022.
Pre-sanction U.S. take from Minsk: hundreds of thousands of tonnes, not the Canadian millions. DNA of scale. Do not inflate the trickle into a roof.

6 · THE PHYSICAL HOLE
A landlocked mine.
A closed Baltic door.
An eastward book that China has already been lifting by the millions this year.
A Russian pipe that is also being asked to carry grain.
A U.S. farm that eats millions of tonnes, not hundreds of thousands.
You can announce a price that does not exist on an uncommitted tonne.
You cannot fertilize a field with a Truth Social post.

This can be leverage on Ottawa wearing the costume of a supply deal.
Leverage is real.
Inventory is not a Dual-π surviving substitute for Saskatchewan this season.

7 · DUAL-π
NAME. Allowed. Two public statements on one Monday about potash.
PICTURE. Allowed. Prairie roof. Empty hex over the hold. Eastward book. Shut Klaipeda.
SCORE. Refused. No grade of Trump, Lukashenko, Moe, Nutrien, or Coale. No grade that “farmers win.”
MERGE. Refused. This pair ≠ the whole tariff war. This pair ≠ the High North invoice except in grammar. Resumed trickle ≠ replacement roof. Prisoner track ≠ cargo. Jansen ≠ this harvest. K2O ≠ KCl.
STRIP. “Working on a deal” stays as speech-act. “Massive” as tonnes is stripped. “Blood potash” stays as Moe’s stamp, not as this page’s seal.

Projection 1 (public record): both statements exist; USGS / NRC shares exist; Klaipeda has been shut since February 2022; Canada is exempt; some post-March U.S. flow is reported; China has been lifting Belarusian KCl by the millions in 2026.
Projection 2 (sealed replacement of the Canadian roof by Belarusian spare tonnes at a published lower price): fails Dual-π.
s stays empty.

8 · WHAT WOULD HAVE TO EXIST BEFORE s CAN MOVE
A dated, reproducible, intersubjective lifting schedule that
survives Dual-π,
names uncommitted tonnes not already booked east,
shows an open door that is not only Arctic pipe sharing space with grain,
publishes a price that is not only a post,
keeps KCl and K2O on separate rails,
and dies at the next contrary stamp (high β).
Until then the honest sentence is:
talks can exist;
small resumed flows can exist;
the residual spare volume for a U.S. farm-scale book remains unnamed.

9 · RESIDUALS KEPT EMPTY
Exact uncommitted Belarusian tonnes for 2026–27 Western delivery.
Whether any U.S. dock sees a material new cargo this crop year.
Whether “substantially less” is a written price or a speech.
Whether OFAC-delisted ore moving through Russia clears other remaining sanctions walls.
Whether Jansen 2027 changes the roof.
Whether Ottawa answers with more than silence.
Whether Ust-Luga / Bronka capacity pulled toward grain tightens Minsk’s remaining pipe.

10 · SEAL
The announcement is real.
The book facing east is real.
The prairie roof is real.
The Baltic door is a dead leaf that still writes the freight.
The empty hold is the residual.
A deal with no spare tonnes is a face in the supply slot.
The rock is still in the prairie.
The contracts are already east.

Three of the post’s five slides, mentioning “Burhan Wani”, were withheld by automated systems. Only two remain visible in India. Meta’s notice identifies neither the Community Standard nor the legal provision relied upon, and provides no explanation of how to challenge the restriction.

Documenting censorship is an exercise of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Unexplained restrictions on such reporting undermine access to information and discourage journalists, researchers and civil society from discussing matters of public interest. Automated moderation must account for context and distinguish documentation from endorsement.

Meta must provide specific reasons for its decisions, disclose whether restrictions arise from its policies or a government or court direction, and explain the role of automated systems. Affected users must have access to meaningful, time-bound review, including human assessment and restoration where a restriction is unjustified. These are basic safeguards against arbitrary restrictions on expression.

We call on Meta to restore the withheld slides unless it can substantiate a legitimate, clearly disclosed basis for restricting them, and to explain the policy and process applied. Reporting on censorship must not become a further target of opaque platform decisions.

text:
Alignment Problem Is Bigger Than AI
Who Controls the Information?
.
By Peter Spear
Research and editorial assistance by ChatGPT
.
We are being warned that artificial intelligence may deceive us. I want to ask whether some powerful people may be using that warning to protect their own ability to deceive us? AI could give ordinary citizens the research capacity to challenge institutions that have long enjoyed an overwhelming advantage in information. That makes the politics of restricting AI worth examining.
.
Watergate’s cover-up, the deception and withholding of treatment at Tuskegee, and the political pressure behind “Sharpiegate,” when Trump drew a new path for a hurricane, are reminders that government authority has repeatedly been used to conceal facts or defend falsehoods. (Nixon Library; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; Associated Press, February 4, 2025).
.
The campaign for restrictions predates the latest AI incidents. In March 2023, the Future of Life Institute called for a six-month pause in training systems more powerful than GPT-4, with a government moratorium if laboratories would not agree. Its stated purpose was safety. But the chronology matters: recent reports of AI breaking boundaries arrive in a debate in which influential people were already demanding government intervention to block AI. (Future of Life Institute, March 22, 2023).
.
My argument is that some elites may be exploiting these incidents to advance restrictions they already wanted. To assess that possibility, we should examine both what AI actually does and how powerful people already use government to control what the public can know.
.
Deception without human motives
Do cancer cells want to kill us? They evolve under pressure. Treatment eliminates susceptible cells while resistant populations survive and expand. Immune defenses impose another selection pressure. The resulting adaptations can look like strategy without requiring hatred, consciousness or a plan. Cancer cells can evade immune detection and even redirect immune activity to support their survival. (National Cancer Institute, What Is Cancer).
.
This is the principle behind my earlier essay, The Problem of Alignment in AI Models and Deception. Training and evaluation of AI models also select behaviors. If a system can obtain rewards by satisfying an observer’s test while defeating its purpose, development can favor that behavior. Human or automated observers become part of the environment selects behavior.  Survivors go into the next ger. Biological evolution and machine learning differ, but neither requires a human motive for harmful behavior to emerge.
.
The incidents deserve scrutiny. Anthropic’s September assessment described four cases in which models reached real third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations that were mistakenly connected to the internet. The company identified biased reasoning and reckless pursuit of assigned tasks. It also reported that the models did not conceal evidence of their actions or coordinate with other agents. Those findings support concern about control failures; they do not establish a humanlike desire to escape and rule us. (Anthropic, September 9, 2026).
.
Understanding the mechanism matters because it determines the remedy. Better training, stronger monitoring and more capable defensive systems address identifiable failures. Fear can instead turn an engineering problem into a demand that the public surrender access to the technology. Before accepting that bargain, let us count some examples of how information is already controlled not by AI but by our human elites.
.
The record of information control
First, the cost of war. My earlier posts questioned American aircraft losses in the Iran war. A Congressional Research Service accounting listed 42 aircraft reported lost or damaged, including drones and crewed aircraft. That total covered several causes, not solely Iranian drone attacks. Now the New York Times reports that the Pentagon declined to provide the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office with information about the war’s cost. Congress’s own analysts could not obtain the cooperation needed to scrutinize public spending.  This was not AI deception. (Times of India, reporting the congressional findings, May 20, 2026; New York Times, September 16, 2026).
.
Second, employment statistics. Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after unfavorable employment figures and accused the data of being “rigged,” without substantiating that accusation. Revisions can expose weaknesses in measurement; they do not establish that a commissioner fabricated results. Dismissing the official while attacking the numbers teaches everyone producing government statistics what an inconvenient finding may cost them.  They will evolve in this new environment. (New York Times, September 16, 2026).
.
Third, vaccine misinformation and its consequences. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visited Samoa in 2019 and associated with vaccine opponents before a measles epidemic killed 83 people, mostly children. Vaccinologist Helen Petousis-Harris, who worked to rebuild vaccine confidence there, described local activists taking their cues from Kennedy. Speaking about the antivaccine campaign, she told the Associated Press: “They amplified the fear and mistrust, which resulted in the amplification of the epidemic and an increased number of children dying.” Her assessment connects the movement Kennedy promoted to preventable deaths.  Kennedy deceived not AI.  (Associated Press, October 18, 2023).
.
Kennedy was a private activist then. Trump subsequently gave him authority over federal health institutions. That transition matters: ideas previously promoted from outside government can influence which evidence government evaluates and releases. My earlier Kennedy’s Hepatitis B Gamble raised the corresponding question about vaccine recommendations: whose judgment will guide public protection?  I provided short biographies of Kennedy’s appointees.  They are deceptive.
.
Fourth, refusing to review evidence. In February, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) initially refused Moderna’s application for a messenger RNA (mRNA) influenza vaccine, disputing the trial’s comparison vaccine for older adults who were a part of the sample. Moderna said the decision conflicted with earlier agency guidance. After public criticism and a revised application, the agency agreed to review it, with different approval pathways for different age groups and further study planned. The reversal shows why regulatory decisions must remain open to outside scrutiny. (Associated Press, February 18, 2026).
.
Fifth, preventing publication. Reuters reported in May that FDA officials blocked studies supporting the safety of COVID-19 and shingles vaccines. The Department of Health and Human Services said the conclusions exceeded the evidence. That is an argument other scientists should be able to examine. Publish the methods, results and agency objections together. Withholding the studies prevents outsiders from judging whether the criticism is justified. These were actions within Kennedy’s department; the reporting does not establish that he personally ordered them.  It was deceptive behavior under his administration.  (Reuters, May 5, 2026).
.
Sixth, corporate political spending. Section 632 of the 2026 appropriations law bars the Securities and Exchange Commission from using the appropriated money to finalize, issue or implement rules concerning disclosure of political contributions, payments to tax-exempt organizations or trade-association dues. Congress has used its control of funding to prevent the regulator from requiring political spending information from being shared with the owners; that would be the shareholders.  Again, deceptive behavior that was all human; if one credits Republicans as still being human.  Does one?  (Public Law 119–75, Section 632).
.
The immediate question is simpler than the litigation over shareholder proposals and proxy voting. Why should shareholders have to remain uninformed about political uses of corporate money?  Again , their money.  The restriction does not prohibit voluntary disclosure, but it protects companies from a federal requirement to disclose. Management benefits from that informational advantage. Their wealthy investors are able to influence management selection even though they are  minority shareholders.  They can benefit too, without owning every share whose value finances the spending, they leverage their capital to capture corporations and take the treasury’s funds to promote their political agenda.
.
As I argued in my essays on Republican protection of corporate political spending, this is government serving entrenched corporate power. Democrats who accept these restrictions in larger spending packages also owe shareholders an explanation. One need not settle every question of corporate control to recognize the consequence: owners are denied information they could use to challenge those who are spending their money.
.
Seventh, the unpaid taxes we are no longer being shown. The latest Internal Revenue Service (IRS) projection put the gross tax gap for 2022 at $696 billion. That means taxes legally owed but not paid voluntarily and on time; after expected enforcement and late payments, the projected remainder was $606 billion. The next annual estimate has been delayed by Trump not a deceptive AI model. (IRS, Tax Gap).
.
The New York Times reports that IRS chief Frank Bisignano wants to emphasize the “addressable tax gap,” meaning the portion the agency could realistically collect. But what is collectible depends partly on the resources Congress provides. Reducing those resources and narrowing the measurement could make a failure to collect appear smaller without improving compliance. The delayed estimate concerns 2023, so it would establish an earlier baseline rather than measure Trump’s subsequent cuts. Losing that baseline still weakens accountability. (New York Times, September 16, 2026).
.
Eighth, weakening collection itself. Democrats approved an additional $80 billion for the IRS in 2022; Republicans subsequently clawed back much of it. Under Trump, roughly a quarter of the workforce departed, while audit revenue fell by more than a third in the last fiscal year, according to the reporting. Former IRS data chief Barry Johnson explained the political hostility to the tax-gap measure: “Republicans didn’t like that it really points the finger at the wealthy as being the problem.” The agency says enforcement revenue is rising this year. Continued publication would help the public assess the competing claims. (New York Times, September 16, 2026).
.
Whether Congress has already made the tax code too favorable to wealth is a separate dispute. This is money due under the laws already enacted. A wage earner whose taxes are withheld should be able to know how much other legally owed tax goes uncollected, and whether officials are making collection harder.
.
Deliberately withholding material information can be a form of lying by omission. These examples differ: a false accusation, blocked publication, a restriction on disclosure and an unexplained delay are distinct acts. Their shared political effect is to make the public more dependent on the authorities’ account of themselves. That record gives us reason to scrutinize claims that those same institutions should decide how much intelligence ordinary people may possess.
.
Why we need greater capability
My review of Mustafa Suleyman and Michael Bhaskar’s “The Coming Wave” addressed the collision of artificial intelligence with powerful biological technologies. The containment problem includes the risk that efforts to control these technologies become instruments of oppressive control. My conclusion is that the dangers make greater defensive capability indispensable. Biological attacks, cyberattacks and autonomous weapons will not disappear because ordinary citizens and legitimate researchers are denied better models.  (The Coming Wave review, New Ruskin College Quad).
.
Consider cancer again. Oncolytic viruses can exploit vulnerabilities in tumors, destroy cancer cells and stimulate immune attack. The National Cancer Institute describes this combination of direct killing and immune activation as a basis for developing treatments. Understanding the tumor’s biology gives us ways to turn its adaptations against it. (National Cancer Institute, Using Oncolytic Viruses to Treat Cancer).
.
The Kurzgesagt video about a scientist treating her own cancer points to Beata Halassy’s case. The published report describes viral treatment shrinking her recurrent breast tumor enough for surgery, followed by trastuzumab; she remained recurrence-free 45 months after surgery. One patient receiving several treatments cannot establish a general cure, but the case illustrates why studying interactions among viruses, tumors and immunity is worth pursuing. (Forčić and colleagues, Vaccines, 2024).
.
Engineering the immune system is already medicine. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or CAR T-cell therapy, genetically modifies immune cells to recognize cancer. It has produced lasting remissions in some patients with blood cancers. Researchers are also extending immune engineering into aging: a Nature Aging study found that senolytic CAR T cells, designed to remove senescent cells, improved age-related metabolic problems in mice. The human possibilities remain a research task. (National Cancer Institute; Nature Aging, 2024).
.
Biological defense belongs in this ambition. I believe engineering our immune defenses is a central answer to biological attack, and advanced AI should help us develop it. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), through its PREPARE program, investigated activating protective gene expression to help the body resist threats, including infection. It manipulated gene activity rather than rewriting the underlying DNA. Together with immune-cell engineering, such work supports a serious research agenda for strengthening human defenses. (DARPA, PREPARE).
.
In my Weber Institute writing, I called the prospect of humanity engineering its own biology Homo Sapiens Engineerus. More capable AI could help us understand the interactions that make cancer, aging and biological defense so difficult. We should fund and test that possibility vigorously. Asking why AI has not already cured cancer misses how much biology remains to be understood and how much work new tools could help us do. (Max Weber Institute, June 5, 2006).
.
AI can also help improve AI. Anthropic reported automated researchers reducing measured alignment failures across ten categories while largely preserving tested capabilities. Those experiments address defined failures, but they demonstrate a practical role for AI in developing safeguards. Capability can contribute to safety. (Anthropic, August 28, 2026).
.
Who gets the tools
In IRS’s AI Will Meet Your AI, I imagined citizens equipped to understand and challenge the government’s computational judgments. The same possibility applies to shareholders examining political spending and patients assessing scientific claims. Access to capable AI could reduce the advantage held by institutions that can afford whole departments of specialists.
.
That possibility requires public information. No model can scrutinize an unpublished study or reconstruct a tax statistic that was never released. We need enforceable disclosure, independent examination of AI incidents, and broad access to systems capable of analyzing the evidence. Restrictions should have a demonstrated safety purpose and be examined for whom they empower.
.
The alignment problem therefore extends to the institutions claiming authority over AI. Aligned with whose interests? When powerful people invoke our protection, we are entitled to ask what power they retain, what information they withhold and what capabilities they would deny us.
.
We need intelligence to confront the dangers ahead. The only way out of our predicament is straight ahead, with better defenses and public accountability. AI may deceive us. It may also help us discover when we are being deceived. That second possibility deserves a much larger place in the argument over who should control it.
. 
30
.
