IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

BIG NEWS 🚨 Login credentials of 149 mn accounts including Gmail, Facebook, Netflix leaked.

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler has discovered an unsecured online database.

149M credentials dumped in an unsecured 96GB database, a "dream wish list for criminals" per researcher Jeremiah Fowler, who stumbled on it while scanning open IPs. We're talking Gmail (millions affected), Facebook, Netflix, Instagram, Roblox, dating sites, even banking logins—likely scraped via infostealer malware like RedLine or Vidar infecting PCs worldwide. No owner ID'd, but it sat exposed for weeks before takedown, amplifying risks of phishing, ID theft, and account takeovers.

Strategic edge: For hackers, this is nitro fuel—credential stuffing attacks could spike 2-3x post-leak, per past patterns (e.g., 2023 RockYou2021 dump). Big Tech's response? Google/FB urging password resets + MFA, but with reuse rates still at 65% globally, it's a ticking bomb. Broader play: Echoes the 2025 mega-breach (184M passwords), showing infostealers evolving faster than defenses—malware now bypasses AV via AI obfuscation.

Indian lens: With 900M+ internet users and digital economy booming (UPI at 15B txn/month), this hits home—est. 10-15M Indian accounts exposed, fueling Aadhaar-linked fraud spikes. Post-DPDP Act rollout in '24, fines could hammer firms, but enforcement gaps persist (CERT-In handled 1.5M incidents in '25 alone). Credit Modi's cybersecurity push—NCCC upgrades cut response times 40%—but without it, we'd be replaying 2022 AIIMS hack. Atmanirbhar angle: Time to pivot to local password managers like PassBolt forks?

Without swift action, expect fraud waves. Thoughts—changed your passwords yet, or waiting for the phish?

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

ARNAB WANTS A BRAVERY MEDAL FOR TRIAL BY MEDIA. THE CONSTITUTION CALLS IT AN ASSAULT ON FAIR TRIAL.

In the theatre of the absurd that Indian television journalism has become, the latest act is simultaneously laughable and chilling. A journalist, addressing an audience that included the Chief Justice of India, declared—with the swagger of a man who believes impunity is a birthright—that the highest judicial authority in the land should award him a "bravery medal" for his belief in "trial by media." 

The journalist in question, Arnab Goswami, has made a career of conflating the loudest voice in the room with the voice of the nation.

Let us be clear at the outset. Trial by media is not a virtue. It is not journalism. It is an assault on the Constitution. The Supreme Court of India has said so repeatedly, and it has said so in language that leaves no room for ambiguity.

The Constitutional Crime Called "Trial by Media"

The right to a fair trial is not a concession granted by the State. It is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that the media cannot be permitted to prejudice the right of defence of an accused in any manner whatsoever.

 In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), the Court observed that every effort must be made to ensure that the distinction between trial by media and informative media is maintained. Trial by media should be avoided particularly at a stage when the suspect is entitled to constitutional protections.

In Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI, the Court held that prior restraint is permissible when necessary to prevent a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the trial. In Navalakha v. Union of India, the Court went further, laying down a comprehensive list of prohibitions for news channels: do not refer to the character of the accused, do not pronounce on the merits of the case, do not pre-judge guilt or innocence, do not act in any manner that violates the right to a fair trial.

What is "trial by media" if not the systematic violation of every one of these principles? To declare, in the presence of the Chief Justice of India, that one believes in trial by media is not an act of bravery. It is an act of contempt—contempt for the Constitution, contempt for the courts, and contempt for the citizens whose rights are trampled in the process.

The Frailty of "Conviction by Soundbyte"

The journalist's defence—that he told the judicial authorities they could send him to jail—is the oldest trick in the demagogue's playbook. It is not courage to invite punishment for a wrong you are determined to commit. That is not the bravery of a soldier facing enemy fire. That is the petulance of a man who believes the rules do not apply to him.

Consider the mechanics of what is being defended. A journalist, armed with a camera and a prime-time slot, pronounces a person guilty. The person has no right to cross-examination. The person has no right to produce evidence. The person has no right to appeal. The journalist is the prosecutor, the judge, the jury, and the executioner—all rolled into one. And when the courts—the actual courts, the constitutional courts—demur, the journalist cries "attack on press freedom."

This is not press freedom. This is press tyranny. And it is precisely the kind of tyranny that the Constitution's framers anticipated when they wrote Article 19(2), which permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interests of the administration of justice.

The Irony of the Bravery Medal:-

The claim for a bravery medal is the most revealing part of the episode. Bravery medals are not given to people who shout the loudest. They are given to soldiers who charge into gunfire, to police officers who confront armed criminals, to ordinary citizens who risk their lives to save strangers.
Continue……

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

DELHI UNION OF JOURNALISTS (Regd.)
Email: duj.delhi@gmail.com

19 September, 2026
Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

The author’s entire bio:

“Arun Agarwal is a civic and business leader in Dallas.”

That leaves out one of the more interesting biographies I’ve come across.

Start in India.

A promotional profile of Agarwal says he earned a B.S. in Jaipur, then an MBA from IMT Ghaziabad and became the “youngest regional manager of JVC Onida for eastern region.”

Only after that, according to the profile, did he leave for America to study computer information systems.

Agarwal told USA Today he came to America in 1990.

But the ages reported for him don’t even agree: D Magazine called him 46 in 2018. Dallas Express called him 51 in 2023. USA Today called him 54 that same year.

Depending which age is correct, Agarwal was roughly 18–21 when he arrived -  after supposedly completing a bachelor’s, an MBA and becoming the youngest regional manager of a major electronics company.

Then there is Anu.

In his account of their story, Anu was a young journalist in Kolkata who encouraged Agarwal to leave India and pursue graduate school in America.

D Magazine said: Anu pushed him toward a master’s in computer information systems, the couple immigrated after he was accepted and after becoming a citizen Agarwal moved to Dallas in 2002 and supposedly “landed a computer analyst job.”

By November 2006, Arun and Anuradha Basu Agarwal were both directors of S2 Resources, an Indian textile/apparel company.

That’s two years before D Magazine says Arun began his textile career with Indian giant Alok Industries in 2008.

And Anu had her own substantial business history. Public biographies identify her as founder and creative director of SAS Group, whose SAS Living operation was described as one of the largest U.S. distributors of furniture and decorative accessories.

The timeline gets stranger.

In a recent Site Selection interview, Agarwal said he “started my own company in textiles here in 2000.”

But another biography says he didn’t move to Dallas until 2002, took the computer analyst job, and joined Alok in 2008.

He later said he “legally separated” the U.S. operation from Alok in 2014 and renamed it Nextt.

Yet D Magazine reported in 2018 that Alok still supplied up to 70% of Nextt’s products and described Nextt as Alok’s “exclusive front-end marketing arm.”

Then Greg Abbott enters the story.

Abbott began appointing Agarwal to state boards in 2016.

That first Governor’s Office bio said his computer-information M.S. came from the University of New Hampshire. Later Abbott bios say Southern New Hampshire University. SNHU was formerly called New Hampshire College - not the University of New Hampshire.

Abbott’s 2019 bio also called Agarwal’s Harvard credential a Master’s in International Business.

By 2022 it was an Advanced Certificate in International Business.

Meanwhile Agarwal became a major Abbott donor, then vice chairman and ultimately chairman of the Texas Economic Development Corporation.

He helped lead Texas economic missions to India and publicly declared:

“Texas is becoming the new IT capital for India.”

His Texas-India work involved companies including Infosys, TCS, Wipro, Tech Mahindra and others.

And then there is Howdy Modi.

Anu & Arun Agarwal were listed as Honorary Committee Co-Chairs. The same event listed longtime HSS leader Ramesh Bhutada as a patron.

I have found no evidence that Agarwal himself belongs to HSS or RSS. The documented point is that his civic and political network overlaps with prominent HSS-linked figures.

So when Arun Agarwal writes about immigration, UT students and displacement, his background seems relevant.

He isn’t merely a “civic and business leader in Dallas.”

He’s an India-born former international student whose own published biography contains conflicting ages, dates, schools, credentials and business timelines; an Abbott donor and appointee; a leader of Texas-India economic development; and a prominent organizer in Indian-American political and business networks.

A nine-word bio leaves out a lot.

text:
DELHI UNION OF JOURNALISTS (Regd.)
Email: duj.delhi@gmail.com

19 September, 2026
Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Dear @noidapolice, @CMOfficeUP the CCTNS portal has multiple issues. I tried filing for tenant verification form online and it challenged me, in some ways saying, “Let me see, how the hell can you file this request, I will show you how sarkari I am!” 

1. Permanent address is pre-selected to UP, meaning I have to put a false UP address to move to next page

2. For a simple jpg file upload, under the recommended size, it kept on returning ‘malicious script found’. Finally, I had to use photoshop, to remove all metadata etc, rename the file and so on! 

3. The tenant info page has two mandatory boxes- Relative name and Relation - can’t write ‘self’, because in ‘relation’ drop down, there is no such thing. 

4. This one is good: After an hour of filling the form, when you hit submit, it goes to ‘processing’ and returns to ‘submit’. I ‘submitted’ it thrice and then thought ‘it must have been submitted. Guess what! No. It doesn’t exist now. No application ID, no service request number, nothing! 

Finally, I asked my property dealer how long it takes for verification, and he was like ‘Sir, kal karwa dunga. Aap ₹500 per person de dena.’ 

I have no choice but to give the details to him for offline application. There is no doubt Digital India is doing wonders, but for some places, the more things change, the more they remain the same. 

No doubt, Noida Police is doing a tremendous job, and I had no intent on tagging them, but this comes under their jurisdiction. Please ask the agency handling it, to make it smooth. I don’t have issues waiting for it to process, but it must do the job efficiently. 

Cc: @ChiefSecyUP @myogiadityanath

Rezaul, a final-year https://t.co/NMjOF3Lwxa student at #AliahUniversity and a resident of Hooghly district’s #Meshera village, was returning from the #BishwaIjtema religious gathering in #Bangladesh along with four friends. The group had boarded a local train from #Gede station to Sealdah when the incident happened.

According to Rezaul, trouble began when a passenger asked him to remove his trolley bag from the luggage rack. He complied without protest, but soon after, a group of men attempted to force him out of his seat. When he resisted, they hurled communal slurs, calling him a “#Bangladeshi.”

“A man named Ajay taunted me, saying, ‘What drove you out of Bangladesh? You’ve come to invade India,’” Rezaul told to media. “I told them I am an Indian citizen, but about a dozen people surrounded me and started attacking me.”

For nearly an hour, Rezaul was repeatedly punched and kicked. His cap was forcibly removed, his hair and beard were pulled, and he was subjected to verbal abuse. At one point, some attackers allegedly urged others to throw him off the moving train.

His friend, Sajid Mirza, attempted to record the assault but was threatened. “They snatched my phone and warned me that if I made a video, they would throw me off the train,” Sajid said. “They accused us of being uneducated militants destroying the country.”

After the attack, Rezaul sought medical treatment before attempting to lodge a complaint at Haripal police station. However, officers allegedly refused to register his case. He later approached the Sealdah Government Railway Police (GRP) on February 5, where his complaint was finally accepted.

A case has been filed under sections 115(2), 299, 351(2), and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and railway police have launched an investigation. “We are looking into the matter, and appropriate legal action will be taken,” a police official said.

The attack has triggered widespread condemnation. Prominent lawyer and Left MP Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya linked the incident to growing communal polarization. “This is not an isolated case. Such acts are happening in states governed by #RSS-backed politics,” he wrote on social media. “Over the past decade, West Bengal has been influenced by RSS ideology, fueling religious divisions. A strong secular movement is needed to break this cycle.”

ISF MLA Peerzada Nawsad Siddique questioned the attackers’ motives: “Was Rezaul assaulted simply because he wore a cap and had a beard? This cannot happen in a democracy.”

Human rights groups, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), also condemned the attack. “This is just the tip of the iceberg. Political parties and sections of the media have turned the state into a communal battleground,” said APDR General Secretary Ranjit Sur.

Mohammad Kamruzzaman of the All Bengal Minority Youth Federation (ABMYF) pointed to a disturbing trend. “Muslim youth have been attacked on trains before. If no action is taken, such incidents will continue,” he warned.

Journalist and activist Moktar Hossain Mondal blamed communal narratives for escalating violence. “Years ago, people were shocked to hear about such attacks on minorities in trains. Now, it’s becoming disturbingly common,” he said.

text:
Honourable Chief Minister Shri A Revanth Reddy attended " The Hindu Huddle " session titled "By, For, and Of the People: Good Governance for Telangana" in Bengaluru on Saturday. 

During conservation with The Hindu Director N Ram, CM Revanth Reddy delved into his political journey from ZPTC member to CM, women empowerment,  job recruitment, political fight with opposition parties, Congress party’s stand on women's reservation.  Union government's indifference towards  Southern India,  Rythu Bharosa, Telangana Rising etc. 

Honourable Chief Minister Shri A @revanth_anumula  alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi resorted to  political gimmicks  on women's reservations in the Legislative bodies. The Congress party was opposed  to linking the women reservation to the increase of  MP seats.  If parliamentary seats are increased as proposed raising Lok Sabha seats in Kerala from 20 to 30 and in Uttar Pradesh from 80 to 120. It would be unjust and this is precisely what we oppose.

WOMEN RESERVATION AND DISCRIMINATION AGAINST SOUTHERN STATES :  

The Congress was demanding the centre not to penalize the performing southern states which  contribute significantly more to the Centre than they receive. The President, Prime Minister, and Union Home Minister all hail from northern states. The 2027 Uttar Pradesh elections are approaching and the centre should prove their sincerity in the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill in the state first.  The Chief Minister appealed to the centre to stop widening the rift between the North and the South parts of the states.

We are the architects of women's reservation policies. Congress governments appointed women Presidents, Lok Sabha Speaker, Governors, and Chief Ministers. Rajiv Gandhi ensured representation for women in local bodies. We passed the Women's Reservation Bill in the Rajya Sabha under Sonia Gandhi's leadership.

VISIT TO CHINA SOON : 

Referring to the investments, the Chief Minister said that Gujarat was not naturally attracting investments, which are being forced into the state.  For the past 20 years, there has been just one brand ambassador working there. Telangana state was not alone competing with neighbouring states and also with the world. Why compete with neighbours only ? We are competing with China, Japan, South Korea, and Germany. My motto is 'China+1'. I visited China 15 years ago and had no hesitation in learning from anyone. I will visit China soon to learn. I once took a ten-day course at Harvard; similarly, I will visit China to understand their best practices.

BLUE COLLAR JOBS AND RECRUITMENT IN GOVERNMENT : 

On the creation of jobs,  CM Revanth Reddy said that blue-collar jobs are an alternative to white-collar jobs. AI has not created an alternative to blue-collar jobs. AI can create many things, but it cannot create a politician. Our youth need to focus on alternatives and enhance their skills. Those who had the opportunity to govern the state in the past viewed themselves merely as rulers; I, however, consider myself a public representative here to serve. There are 2 lakh vacant government jobs in Telangana and his government started recruitment. We provided 67,760 jobs in just 15 months—the highest number of jobs provided anywhere in the country. We issued notifications two weeks ago, and a notification for the recruitment of 5,000 police personnel will be issued soon. Our youth are now preparing for these jobs. The recruitment agency Telangana Public Service Commission was also revamped. During KCR rule, an RMP doctor served as a member of the commission and interviewed Group-1 candidates. Is an RMP doctor the right person to oversee appointments for engineers, doctors, and other professional roles?. the CM averred.

TELANGANA RISING 2047  :

 Elaborating the comprehensive plan for Telangana development  to achieve a $1 trillion economy by 2034 and a $3 trillion economy by 2047, the CM said that the state has been divided into 3 zones. The urban area within the 160-km Outer Ring Road (ORR) as CURE (Core Urban Region Economy),  the area between the ORR and the Regional Ring Road (RRR) is called PURE (Peri-Urban Region Economy) and beyond the RRR as RARE (Rural Agricultural Region Economy). We held a global summit on December 7, 8, and 9 last year and released a policy document. We are prioritizing the service sector in CURE, manufacturing in PURE, and agriculture in RARE. We intend to transform CURE into a 'Net Zero' city and are implementing plans aligned with this policy. Even though we are incurring an annual loss of ₹2,000 crore, we decided to mandate the use of electric vehicles (EVs) within the CURE zone and waived taxes on EVs.  We are undertaking Metro expansion and restoring lakes by removing encroachments. Constructing water harvesting wells and promoting the manufacturing sector within the region and also  building 'Bharat Future City' across 30,000 acres and inviting Fortune 500 companies to invest here. Since the Telangana state is a landlocked state, the CM said that he was consulting with Prime Minister Modi and the Chief Minister of the neighboring state, Chandrababu Naidu, to connect the Machilipatnam port via a 12-lane highway.

 We are striving to establish seamless connectivity through road, rail, port, and airport networks, as these will drive our growth. We are home to institutions like ISB, IIIT, and NALSAR University; we have focused on educational institutions and recognized the importance of human resources.  We are all discussing AI these days; AI is causing the loss of white-collar jobs. That is why we established the Young India Skills University—a public-private partnership. Anand Mahindra serves as the Chairman, and Srini Raju as the Vice-Chairman. We have transformed our ITIs into Advanced Technology Centres (ATCs) at a cost of ₹2,400 crore.  The Tata company is contributing 86 percent  and creating blue-collar jobs. I have  frequently visited Germany, Japan, and South Korea to study how blue-collar jobs are taking the place of white-collar jobs. Those in blue-collar roles earn more than IT engineers.  We are providing training in German, Japanese, and Korean languages to enable people to work in those countries. 

CENTRE’s INDIFFERENCE TOWARDS TELANGANA : 

The Chief minister criticized the union government for not extending financial assistance and also discriminated against  Telangana in approving investments.  In the past, short-term loans were secured at interest rates of 11 per cent  to 11.50 per cent. We are currently restructuring them with interest rates of 7 to 8 percent and converting them into long-term loans. We are in the process of restructuring debts worth ₹2 lakh crore. Neither the Centre nor the states are focusing on the flaws within the GST system. We have appointed Arvind Subramanian as a GST advisor. Over the past 7–8 years, monthly GST revenue never exceeded ₹3,500 crore, but for the last six months, it has crossed the ₹4,000 crore mark. We have generated an additional ₹5,000 crore in just six months. This was achieved by curbing corruption and plugging revenue leakages, without raising taxes.  We will fight against the Central Government's discrimination. Regarding investment approvals for our state, they are directing investors to go to Gujarat instead and this is the situation we are facing.

FARMERS – LOAN WAIVER :

 CM Revanth Reddy  highlighted the  measures taken for rescuing the distressed farmers for the last two years.   In the past, Telangana recorded the highest number of farmer suicides after Maharashtra, primarily due to debt. The Congress government waived loans amounting to ₹20,616 crore for 25,035 farming families which is the largest loan waiver in the country. An NCRB report—a report by the Central Government—stated that Telangana was a state with zero farmer suicides in the 2024-25 year. Farmers are happy. Previously, farmers had to struggle for the Minimum Support Price (MSP). Now,  we  ensured the MSP and also provided a bonus of ₹500 per quintal to paddy farmers. The Centre is neglecting crop procurement.  They simply announce the MRP and wash their hands of the matter. We are procuring Paddy and Maize, alongside others. Under the 'Rythu Bharosa' scheme, we provide ₹12,000 per acre, which farmers utilize for fertilizers and cultivation expenses.

WOMEN EMPOWERMENT : 

The Chief minister said that economic assistance is being provided to 6.7 million women in self-help groups across Telangana. They have availed loans worth ₹60,000 crore at zero interest, with the government bearing the interest costs. Women's groups have purchased 1,000 buses and also ventured into the renewable energy sector.  The government  has also allocated petrol bunks and solar plants to them. Members of these women's groups operate canteens at various government institutions, and we have entrusted them with the task of creating facilities in government schools.

REFORMS IN  EDUCATION :

 A slew of  measures were taken to strengthen the education in the  public sector,  the CM said that  we are introducing pre-schools. We have 27,000 government schools catering to 1.8 million (18 lakh) children, while there are 12,000 private schools with 3.5 million (35 lakh) children. Government teachers are highly qualified and many hold MA and PhD degrees. Yet, the children were not enrolling because  of lack of pre-school facilities.  We are also providing transport along with breakfast and mid-day meals to the students and sending the teachers to Singapore and other countries for study tours.

BUREAUCRACY :  

CM Revanth Reddy asserted that “ common sense is a crucial element of administration. If a problem is understood through common sense, half the  problem is solved and the rest is resolved through appropriate decision-making. If he  makes an opinion first, they tend to align their responses with it trying to please me. I spent 17 years in the opposition, from 2006 to 2023. During that time, I learned a great deal and fought for public causes. It was the reason no one can mislead me.

HYDRAA- LAKES  PROTECTION : 

The government's initiative  to protect the lakes and water bodies from the encroachments was discussed in the conversation. The Chief Minister said that  the government has established HYDRAA to remove all encroachments.  A senior IPS officer was appointed as the head of the  HYDRAA. Further, the CM said that    there are six major metropolitan cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru. Each of these cities should follow its own model to solve the encroachments, as well as strategies for environmental issues, water scarcity, and flash floods.

DRUG MENACE: 

Aiming to promote Telangana  as a drug free state , CM Revanth Reddy said that the 'Eagle Force' was set up to combat the drug menace, as students are falling victim to drugs. Our Eagle Force is the best in the country and our goal is to eradicate the drug problem completely.

CASTE CENSUS : 

The BC, SC, ST and minorities' welfare was given top priority in the government, the chief minister said that the main objective was to eliminate differences based on caste in education. The previous governments established separate residential schools for SCs, STs, BCs, and minorities. To truly eliminate casteism and foster unity without social barriers, we are now establishing 'Young India Integrated Schools' .   Following the Supreme Court's verdict, we also  implemented the categorization of SCs in our state. Even Gujarat has not implemented the Supreme Court's ruling . A caste census has not been conducted in the country since 1931. We conducted a caste census in our state; how can you extend welfare schemes to Backward Classes (BCs) without a caste census?

To a question,  the CM clarified that he does not resort to abuse and speaks sarcastically. He never argued with journalists and threatened any one for writing against him. He viewed the media as a source of 'back-office' information. He also regularly holds press conferences every ten days and answers every question asked. The CM emphasized that true understanding comes only from connecting with the people. Connecting with the public is the real strength in public life.

POLITICAL JOURNEY :

CM Revanth Reddy narrated how he grew in politics as a leader of the student wing (Vidyarthi Parishad),  ventured into business and later elected as an  independent ZPTC member and MLC in  2007. Subsequently, he  joined the TDP and worked under the leadership of Chandrababu Naidu for ten years. He  was elected as an MLA twice. Due to the state bifurcation and local factors, he resigned from the TDP.  At that time, he  had several options before him but decided to join the Congress party because it was the Congress that granted statehood to Telangana.  Sonia Gandhi fulfilled the 60-year-old dream of the people of Telangana. When he  joined the party, he  apprised Rahul Gandhi of every detail regarding my political journey. He  became the PCC President and the Chief Minister. By July 2026, he will have completed 20 years in public life. Throughout his  political career, he has fought for the people and the common man. He came from an agricultural family and his father was a Police Patel. Without any political background or backing,  ours is a family defined by a strong work ethic. He reached this position thanks to the blessings of the people of Telangana.
@the_hindu

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

After months of building this initiative for mass adoption across India (feeding it nationwide PM-to-ward-level representative data) and getting very close to public release, I received a notice from MeitY
My DNS was eventually taken down ( it's been 45 days). The concern raised was that I was using photos and information of ministers and public representatives for features such as Certificate of Shame and Leader Geotag photos.

I’m currently working through the issue with the authorities. But I also have another plan to relaunch this.

Before I reveal it, here’s what makes this project fundamentally different and why taking down a single website doesn’t actually take down the application.
I built the entire application on the Internet Computer #ICP  blockchain. The application logic and data live on-chain.

The app is still accessible through its native blockchain URL, but that URL isn’t human-friendly. So I connected it to a Web2 domain: https://t.co/ihjT4pIcBF.

The government can block the Web2 domain but they can't simply "take down" the application that exists on the blockchain.

And this highlights one of the biggest missing pieces of the decentralized web: on-chain DNS.

The ICP ecosystem is already moving in this direction, with the broader vision around DNSSEC, NNS and Chain-Key technology. ( @dominic_w @PierreSamaties

A woman employee at Tech Mahindra Dundigal campus, Hyderabad, says she was terminated after taking three days of leave to care for her sick 11 year old daughter.

But the story gets worse.

She had reportedly joined the company only about four and a half months earlier. 

Before this, she says she had taken around 14 days of medical leave after falling ill and being hospitalised and received repeated emails asking her to return to work.

When her daughter fell ill, she informed her supervisors that she needed three days off.

She says she was asked to log in and wait for approval, but left after repeated calls from her daughter and informed the company that she would make up the work.

She later received instructions to report back, followed by a termination notice. 

She has since filed a police complaint and protested outside the company's campus. Police have begun a preliminary inquiry.

Tech Mahindra says it has contacted her and is reviewing the matter urgently.

So, to be precise, she alleges she was terminated because she took leave to care for her sick child. That allegation is being investigated and it is not yet an established finding.

But the question this case raises is bigger than one employee.

What happens to working mothers when family emergency becomes a workplace liability?

Companies can have targets, deadlines and attendance policies. But if a mother has to choose between her sick child and her job, what exactly are we calling family friendly or this entire charade of women back to workplace?

And if corporate India wants women to stay in the workforce, it cannot treat caregiving as an inconvenience that employees must somehow hide.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document.
